exact_title: Dysregulated adult hippocampal neurogenesis in major depressive disorder
verification_notes: Verified against the primary paper (DOI 10.1038/s41591-026-04571-8, Nature Medicine, 2026-08-21): title, journal, study design (multiomic postmortem human hippocampal tissue study), sample composition across the three assay types, primary outcome, main result, and major limitations all confirmed. pmid not yet assigned/found. sample_size is left null rather than collapsed into one number because the source reports three distinct assay-level cohorts (snMultiome, spatial, proteomics) with different Ns; the breakdown is recorded in study_design/population instead. funding and conflicts_of_interest were not established in the prior audit and remain null.
study_design: Multiomic postmortem human hippocampal tissue study using single-nucleus RNA-seq/ATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics and proteomics. Primary snMultiome analysis: 11 MDD and 19 control samples retained after QC. Spatial analysis: 9 MDD and 11 control biological samples. Proteomics: 12 MDD and 12 control individuals.
population: Postmortem human hippocampal tissue from nonmedicated major depressive disorder donors and neurotypical controls.
primary_outcome: Neurogenic-lineage cell proportions and gene-regulatory activity across the hippocampal neurogenic trajectory.
main_result: MDD hippocampi showed a shift toward more quiescent early-stage progenitors and fewer neuroblasts, consistent with a stalled rather than absent neurogenic trajectory.
major_limitations: Postmortem; cross-sectional; cannot establish whether altered neurogenesis causes or results from MDD; small donor sample; differences in recent stress exposure may confound interpretation.
why_now: Recently published human multiomic evidence relevant to the longstanding scientific debate around adult hippocampal neurogenesis and depression.
proposed_title: Depression and Your Brain's Missing Neurons: What Postmortem Tissue Actually Shows
best_video_angle: Explain what the postmortem data show while explicitly separating association from causal direction.
